lie: I will build a great, great wall on our southern border, and I will have Mexico pay for that wall. Mark my words.
fallacy: Broken Promise / Unfulfilled Commitment — The wall was not fully built and Mexico never paid for any portion of it.

lie: I won the popular vote by a tremendous margin. We had a massive landslide victory in the Electoral College.
fallacy: Falsehood / Fabrication — Hillary Clinton won the popular vote by approximately 2.9 million votes.

lie: I think we've had the largest audience ever to witness an inauguration — period — both in person and around the globe.
fallacy: Exaggeration / False Comparison — Aerial photos and transit data showed attendance was significantly lower than the 2009 inauguration of Barack Obama.

lie: We are also getting rid of the Defense sequester, which is a very, very important thing. … Because of our military spending bill, what was being done, we are going to be doing a lot more than we were doing before.
fallacy: Falsehood — The 2018 budget preserved the Budget Control Act spending caps; no sequester was eliminated.

lie: And the day before, voter fraud — 3 to 5 million people, people that are dead. And I won by a massive, massive margin. They said 3 to 5 million.
fallacy: Baseless Accusation / Straw Man — No credible evidence of 3 to 5 million fraudulent votes has ever been presented; multiple studies found no widespread fraud.

lie: The murder rate in our country is the highest it's been in 45 to 50 years.
fallacy: Falsehood — FBI data showed the U.S. murder rate in 2016 was near historic lows, not at a 45–50 year high.

lie: Obama had his eight years, and he didn't do it. He didn't do it. I don't know why. He talked about it. But he didn't do it.
fallacy: Misrepresentation — The Affordable Care Act was a major legislative achievement of the Obama administration; the claim ignores that record.

lie: Last year, the trade deficit with China was roughly $500 billion. This is not a free trade situation. It's foolish trade. It's stupid trade.
fallacy: Exaggeration — The actual U.S. trade deficit with China in 2017 was approximately $375 billion, not $500 billion.

lie: I never said the repeal and replace of Obamacare would be easy. I said it would be tough — very tough. But we're going to get it done.
fallacy: Falsehood — On multiple occasions Trump said repealing and replacing Obamacare would be easy, including in March 2017 statements.

lie: We have it under control. It's going to be just fine. … It's one person coming in from China, and we have it under control. It's going to be just fine.
fallacy: False Reassurance / Wishful Thinking — The COVID-19 outbreak escalated into a global pandemic that the U.S. was not prepared for.

lie: It is going to disappear. It is disappearing.
fallacy: Wishful Thinking / False Reassurance — COVID-19 did not 'disappear' and continued to spread widely in the following months.

lie: If we didn't catch the case early, and if we didn't do the right things, it would have been a mass death — a mass death like you have never seen in this country.
fallacy: Contradiction — This statement directly contradicts his earlier claims that the virus was 'under control' and 'disappearing.'

lie: The 2020 election was rigged. We won by a landslide. This was a stolen election.
fallacy: Baseless Accusation / Big Lie — Dozens of courts, state election officials, and the Justice Department found no evidence of widespread fraud; Joe Biden won the election.

lie: I am a very stable genius.
fallacy: Self-Serving Bias / Non-Sequitur — An unsupported self-assessment that adds no evidence to refute the underlying questions about his fitness.

lie: I don't take any responsibility at all.
fallacy: Evasion of Responsibility — A commander-in-chief's statement during an escalating public health crisis, contradicting the expected role of leadership.

lie: The Mexican government … they send the bad ones over.
fallacy: Pants on Fire / Fabrication — No evidence shows the Mexican government encourages criminals to cross the border; most illegal immigration is people seeking work, and Mexican immigration had dropped sharply during and after the recession.

lie: Our real unemployment is anywhere from 18 to 20 percent. Don't believe the 5.6. Don't believe it.
fallacy: Falsehood / Exaggeration — The official U-6 underemployment rate was 10.8%; even the most expansive alternative measures could not plausibly exceed 16%, and the actual rate was 5.5%, not 5.6%.

lie: Even our nuclear arsenal doesn't work. It came out recently they have equipment that is 30 years old. They don't know if it worked.
fallacy: Falsehood — Recent lapses in the U.S. nuclear program involved personnel and command-and-control problems, not equipment that 'doesn't work.' The Pentagon and Energy Department annually certify the arsenal as safe, secure, and effective.

lie: Last quarter, it was just announced our gross domestic product … was below zero. Whoever heard of this? It's never below zero.
fallacy: Pants on Fire / Falsehood — GDP growth has been below zero 42 times since 1946; the economy itself is in the trillions of dollars and never near zero.

lie: When was the last time you saw a Chevrolet in Tokyo? It doesn't exist, folks. They beat us all the time.
fallacy: Mostly False / Exaggeration — Chevrolet sold 597 cars in Japan in 2014; the brand exists there, even if sales are small. The U.S.–Japan auto trade imbalance is real, but the absolute claim of nonexistence is false.

lie: Islamic terrorism is eating up large portions of the Middle East. … They just built a hotel in Syria. Can you believe this? They built a hotel.
fallacy: Falsehood — ISIS did not build a hotel; it seized an existing hotel in Iraq and uses it to house commanders, not to attract paying guests.

lie: I write a book called The Art of the Deal, the No. 1 selling business book of all time, at least I think, but I'm pretty sure it is.
fallacy: Falsehood / Self-Aggrandizement — Nielsen BookScan data shows The Art of the Deal has sold roughly 177,000–184,000 copies since 2001, far fewer than multiple other business titles (e.g., The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People, Built to Last, The One Minute Manager).

lie: You have illegal immigrants pouring through the country. … They're incarcerated. Many of them are in jails. You have hundreds of thousands of people going to state and federal penitentiaries. That just came out in a Homeland Security Report.
fallacy: Falsehood / Fabricated Statistic — Homeland Security confirmed it does not regularly track the incarcerated illegal-immigrant population, and no such report exists. Bureau of Justice Statistics data shows roughly 90,000 noncitizens in state and federal prisons at year-end 2013, not 'hundreds of thousands.'

lie: I don't think that [11 million] is an accurate number anymore. I am now hearing it's 30 million, it could be 34 million, which is a much bigger problem.
fallacy: Pants on Fire — Every credible estimate (Department of Homeland Security, Pew, Center for Migration Studies) puts the unauthorized immigrant population at roughly 11 million, with a margin of error of about one million. No researcher has published a number near 30 million.

lie: We have a real unemployment rate that's probably 21%. … Because you have ninety million people that aren't working. Ninety-three million to be exact. If you start adding it up, our real unemployment rate is 42%.
fallacy: Pants on Fire / Falsehood — Even the most expansive alternative unemployment measures top out near 16.4%; the figure appears to conflate the labor-force participation rate (the share of adults not in the labor force, including retirees, students, and stay-at-home parents) with unemployment.

lie: Look, we're the most highly taxed nation in the world — that's why taxes have to go down, business has to come back, jobs have to be back.
fallacy: Falsehood — The U.S. total tax burden was about 26% of GDP in 2014, well below most OECD peers; even on corporate tax rates, the U.S. statutory rate was the highest but its effective rate was not. The U.S. is not 'the most highly taxed nation in the world' on any common measure.

lie: I am the only person on this dais — the only person — that fought very, very hard against us … going into Iraq. … I was so vocal about it. … A delegation was sent to my office to see me because I was so vocal about it.
fallacy: Falsehood / Self-Serving Bias — On September 11, 2002 (six months before the invasion), Trump told Howard Stern he supported invading Iraq ('Yeah, I guess so.'). His earliest known public criticism came in an August 2004 Esquire interview — 17 months after the war began. There is no evidence of a Bush White House delegation to 'silence' him.

lie: You take this little beautiful baby and you pump it with what looks like it's meant for a horse, not a child. … I am totally in favor of vaccines. But I want smaller doses over a longer period of time. … I believe autism will go way down.
fallacy: Pants on Fire / False Cause — Decades of epidemiological research, including CDC studies and the Institute of Medicine, have found no link between vaccines and autism. Spreading out doses beyond the recommended schedule has no demonstrated benefit and increases the window of susceptibility to disease.

lie: The unemployment rate is probably 20 percent, but I will tell you, you have some great economists that will tell you it's a 30, 32. And the highest I've heard so far is 42 percent.
fallacy: Pants on Fire — No recognized economist or government statistic supports a 42% unemployment rate. The figure traces to a column by David Stockman counting retirees, students, stay-at-home parents, and people with disabilities as 'unemployed.'

lie: I watched when the World Trade Center came tumbling down. And I watched in Jersey City, N.J., where thousands and thousands of people were cheering as that building was coming down. Thousands of people were cheering.
fallacy: Pants on Fire / Fabricated Event — Exhaustive searches of contemporary newspaper and broadcast records (including LexisNexis and the AP) found no evidence — and certainly no video — of 'thousands' of New Jersey residents celebrating on 9/11. The closest items were a few uncorroborated rumors, debunked at the time.

lie: [Tweet graphic, 'USA Crime Statistics–2015':] 'Whites killed by whites — 16%. Whites killed by blacks — 81%.'
fallacy: Pants on Fire / False Statistics — FBI data show the opposite of what the graphic claimed: in 2014, about 82% of white homicide victims were killed by whites and about 15% by blacks. The graphic also misrepresented every other racial category, and cited a nonexistent 'Crime Statistics Bureau.'

lie: The border city of El Paso, Texas, used to have extremely high rates of violent crime — one of the highest in the country, and considered one of our nation's most dangerous cities. Now, immediately upon its building, with a powerful barrier in place, El Paso is one of the safest cities in our country. Simply put, walls work and walls save lives.
fallacy: Falsehood / False Cause — El Paso was never among the nation's most dangerous cities: its violent crime rate ran well below the national average for cities of its size, and crime had been falling since 1993 — years before the border fence was built in 2008–09. Violent crime actually ticked up in the years immediately after the fence went up.

lie: No Collusion, No Obstruction, Complete and Total EXONERATION. KEEP AMERICA GREAT!
fallacy: Misrepresentation / Falsehood — Special Counsel Robert Mueller's report did not exonerate Trump on obstruction; it stated that while it did not conclude the president committed a crime, 'it also does not exonerate him.' Mueller took no position on obstruction, leaving the question to the attorney general.

lie: If you have a windmill anywhere near your house, congratulations, your house just went down 75 percent in value. And they say the noise causes cancer. You tell me that one, okay?
fallacy: Baseless Claim / Falsehood — There is no evidence that wind turbine noise causes cancer; the American Cancer Society says it is 'unaware of any credible evidence' linking the two, and a literature review found none. The 75% property-value drop is also unsupported by data.

lie: President Obama separated the children. … I'm the one that stopped it.
fallacy: Misattribution / Falsehood — The family separations at the border resulted from the Trump administration's own 'zero-tolerance' policy, which directed federal prosecutors to charge all adults caught crossing illegally and placed their children in separate detention. The Obama administration had no such blanket policy.

lie: We're charging China tariffs. We've never taken in 10 cents from China, and now we're taking in billions and billions of dollars.
fallacy: Misrepresentation / Falsehood — Tariffs are not paid by China; they are paid by American importers and, ultimately, U.S. businesses and consumers. The U.S. goods trade deficit with China hit a record roughly $419 billion in 2018, not the '10 cents' Trump claimed.

lie: Then, I have an Article II, where I have the right to do whatever I want as president. But, I don't even talk about that because they did a report and there was no obstruction.
fallacy: Misrepresentation — Article II of the Constitution does not give the president authority to do 'whatever I want.' It vests executive power subject to checks from Congress and the courts, and no legal basis supports the claim of unlimited presidential discretion.

lie: In addition to Florida — South Carolina, North Carolina, Georgia, and Alabama, will most likely be hit (much) harder than anticipated.
fallacy: Falsehood / Fabrication — The National Weather Service in Birmingham corrected Trump within 20 minutes, stating Alabama would see no impacts from Hurricane Dorian. No official forecast put Alabama in the storm's path; Trump later displayed a NOAA map that had been altered with a black marker to extend the track into Alabama, in what became known as 'Sharpiegate.'

lie: People are flushing toilets 10 times, 15 times as opposed to once. They end up using more water. The EPA is looking at that very strongly at my suggestion.
fallacy: Falsehood / Exaggeration — There is no data to support the claim that Americans flush toilets 10 to 15 times per use, or that low-flow fixtures force repeated flushing. Federal efficiency standards have cut average water use per flush by roughly half without any documented 10-fold flushing problem.

lie: It's going to disappear. One day — it's like a miracle — it will disappear.
fallacy: Falsehood / Baseless Prediction — COVID-19 did not disappear. The WHO had already warned the virus had 'pandemic potential,' and by year-end the U.S. had recorded more than 300,000 deaths. Epidemiologists said there was no basis to expect a respiratory virus that had gained such a foothold to simply vanish on its own.

lie: Yeah, no, I don't take responsibility at all, because we were given a set of circumstances and we were given rules, regulations, and specifications from a different time.
fallacy: Deflection / Scapegoating — The slow coronavirus testing rollout was the responsibility of the Trump administration, which controlled the CDC's test design, approval and distribution throughout his term. A member of his own task force called the testing 'a failing,' and the claim that pre-existing rules were the cause gave no factual basis for dodging accountability.

lie: And then I see the disinfectant, where it knocks it out in a minute. One minute. And is there a way we can do something like that, by injection inside or almost a cleaning.
fallacy: Falsehood / Dangerous Conjecture — Injecting or ingesting disinfectants cannot treat COVID-19 and is extremely hazardous; doctors, poison-control experts and disinfectant manufacturers all issued urgent warnings against ingesting or injecting cleaning products. Trump later claimed the remarks were 'sarcastic,' but the White House transcript and video show no such framing at the time.

lie: I'm taking it — hydroxychloroquine. Right now. Yeah. A couple of weeks ago, I started taking it. ... I'm not going to get hurt by it.
fallacy: Falsehood / False Cause — Hydroxychloroquine is an unproven treatment for COVID-19 and was not shown to prevent infection. The FDA cautioned against using it outside hospitals or clinical trials and revoked its emergency use authorization in June after a large randomized trial found no benefit and possible heart risks.

lie: Mail-In Ballots will lead to massive electoral fraud and a rigged 2020 Election.
fallacy: Falsehood / Misrepresentation — Widespread mail-in voting is long-established — used for years by the military and as the default in states like Oregon, Washington and Colorado — and studies consistently find voter fraud of any kind to be extraordinarily rare. Describing it as inherently fraudulent was baseless and, notably, ignored that Trump himself had voted by mail in Florida.

lie: Proud Boys, stand back and stand by. But I'll tell you what: somebody's got to do something about antifa and the Left.
fallacy: Misrepresentation / Evasion — Pressed repeatedly to condemn white supremacist and militia groups, Trump instead addressed the Proud Boys — a far-right group designated a hate group — with 'stand back and stand by,' and falsely cast violence as coming 'from the left wing.' The Proud Boys celebrated the remark as tacit encouragement.

lie: That means I can't get it (immune), and can't give it. Very nice to know!!!
fallacy: Falsehood / Overreach — No medical basis supported certainty of immunity. Reinfection cases had already been documented and immunity duration was unknown. Trump's own care — an experimental antibody cocktail plus the steroid dexamethasone — offered no guarantee of immunity and, per experts, might even have suppressed his natural antibody response.

lie: Frankly, we did win this election... So we'll be going to the U.S. Supreme Court. We want all voting to stop.
fallacy: Falsehood / Premature Declaration — Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election by 306 electoral votes to 232. On election night millions of legal ballots remained uncounted, and counting valid votes is not fraud; no evidence of widespread fraud was ever produced, and Trump's own administration officials found none.

lie: We won Georgia easily. We won it by hundreds of thousands of votes. But if you go by basic, simple numbers, we won it easily, easily.
fallacy: Falsehood / Misrepresentation — On a recorded call, Trump tried to persuade Georgia's secretary of state to 'find' him votes, insisting he won the state by 'hundreds of thousands.' The certified results, counted three times (including a hand recount), showed Biden won Georgia by 11,779 votes. Raffensperger told Trump directly: 'The data you have is wrong.'

lie: We won. We won in a landslide. This was a landslide.
fallacy: Falsehood / Premature Declaration — Speaking on the Ellipse before his supporters marched on the Capitol, Trump again claimed victory. He had lost: Biden won 306 electoral votes to 232 and the national popular vote by about 7 million. All 50 states certified results, election officials found no significant fraud, and none of 62 lawsuits Trump filed proved any fraud affecting the outcome.

lie: Hydroxychloroquine works.
fallacy: Falsehood / False Cause — Trump topped his 'I was right about everything' list with a fringe study. Hydroxychloroquine has never been shown to treat or prevent COVID-19: the FDA revoked its emergency authorization in June 2020, and large randomized trials (RECOVERY, WHO SOLIDARITY) found no benefit — the RECOVERY trial found it increased mortality risk. The study Trump cited was an unvetted preprint.

lie: This means we (you!) won the Presidential Election in Georgia. The 2020 presidential election was rigged!
fallacy: Falsehood / Misrepresentation — Trump claimed Georgia's routine plan to remove about 101,789 outdated voter files (mostly people who moved) proved he won. Federal law requires states to purge rolls in non-federal years; Georgia removed 290,000 voters in 2019 and about 100,000 in 2021. The roughly 5 million Georgia ballots were counted three times, affirming Biden's 11,779-vote win.

lie: So many incredible facts have now come out to show conclusively that [the election] wasn't [legitimate].
fallacy: Falsehood / Begging the Question — Trump asserted the election was illegitimate without evidence. A Republican-led Michigan Senate committee found 'no evidence of widespread or systemic fraud'; courts repeatedly rejected Trump's claims; and officials, including his own attorney general Bill Barr, confirmed there was no fraud on a scale to alter the outcome. No evidence emerged in any state to reverse the result.

lie: In Springfield (Ohio), they're eating the dogs, the people that came in, they're eating the cats. They're eating, they're eating the pets of the people that live there.
fallacy: Falsehood / Misrepresentation — Speaking at the presidential debate, Trump repeated a baseless claim about Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio. Springfield police and city officials said there were no credible reports of pets being harmed. The rumor traced to an unverified social-media post. PolitiFact named it its 2024 Lie of the Year.

lie: We have 13,099, exactly. … These are people that were in prison, and they're murderers. Some are up for the death penalty but some killed far more than one person. … Every one of them has been released into the United States of America.
fallacy: Falsehood / Misrepresentation — Trump implied 13,099 undocumented convicted murderers were set loose by the Biden-Harris administration. The figure is the number of noncitizens convicted of murder who were not ICE-detained — most entered the U.S. before Biden took office, and many were in prisons and jails, not 'on the loose.' It does not reflect anyone released by the current administration.

lie: A lot of talk about massive CHEATING in Philadelphia. Law Enforcement coming!!!
fallacy: Falsehood / Conspiracy Theory — Hours before polls closed on Election Day, Trump alleged 'massive cheating' in Philadelphia. No evidence supported the claim; local and state election officials confirmed normal vote-counting procedures. Police reported no intrusion; federal and state authorities found none. The false post echoed his debunked 2020 claims.

lie: I know nothing about Project 2025. I have no idea who is behind it. I disagree with some of the things they're saying and some of the things they're saying are absolutely ridiculous and abysmal. Anything they do, I wish them luck, but I have nothing to do with them.
fallacy: Misrepresentation / Evasion — Trump claimed total ignorance of Project 2025, a right-wing transition blueprint. CNN identified at least 140 former Trump-administration officials involved in the project, many of his platform items overlapped with its proposals, and his campaign printed an agenda aligned with its goals. The blanket denial misrepresented the depth of his ties.

lie: We had a landslide election. … We won every swing state. We won the popular vote by millions and millions of people. Nobody even knows how many people, millions, and they're still counting in some areas.
fallacy: Falsehood / Misrepresentation — A day after Congress certified his 2024 victory, Trump claimed votes were 'still counting.' All states had certified results in November or December, the Electoral College voted, and Congress accepted them Jan. 6. His popular-vote margin was about 2.3 million — not unknowable 'millions and millions.' Remaining state-race litigation is not ballot counting.

lie: And we also want them to release the water. If they released the water, they wouldn't have had a problem. If they released the water when I told them to … you might not have even had a fire.
fallacy: Falsehood / False Cause — Trump claimed California's Southern wildfires could have been prevented if more water were released from the north, and threatened to condition federal aid on the state enacting voter ID and water changes. Experts attributed the blazes to extreme drought and Santa Ana winds; there is no water 'spigot' that can fight wildfires, and California already requires ID to register to vote.

lie: Over the past four years, 21 million people poured into the United States. Many of them were murderers, human traffickers, gang members, and other criminals from the streets of the world's most dangerous cities due to Joe Biden's insane and very dangerous open border policies.
fallacy: Falsehood / Misrepresentation — Trump's '21 million' conflated border encounters with unique people entering — the same person can be stopped multiple times. CBP recorded roughly 14 million encounters over the four years, not 21 million arrivals. And the broad claim that many migrants are murderers, traffickers or gang members is unsupported: studies consistently show immigrants commit crime at lower rates than native-born Americans.

lie: Elon [Musk] is helping the Doge team to find billions and billions of dollars in waste, fraud and abuse. … including $8 million for making mice transgender.
fallacy: Falsehood / Misrepresentation — In his address to Congress, Trump said the government spent $8 million 'making mice transgender.' The NIH-funded studies merely examined how gender-affirming hormones affect conditions such as asthma, immunity and breast-cancer risk — standard medical research, not research to 'make mice transgender.' The figure itself was drawn from a watchdog report that overstated the grants.

lie: [Medical professionals] are sterilizing a growing number of impressionable children.
fallacy: Falsehood / Exaggeration — Trump's executive order claimed gender-affirming care is 'sterilizing a growing number of impressionable children.' Gender-affirming surgery on minors is very rare — particularly irreversible genital surgeries — and, under major medical associations, only the most severe cases receive care. The order, which framed these procedures as 'junk science,' was later partly blocked by federal judges.

lie: I was proudly responsible for the ending of something that all legal scholars, both sides, wanted, and in fact demanded: Roe v. Wade. They wanted it ended.
fallacy: Falsehood / Overgeneralization — Trump claimed 'all legal scholars, both sides' wanted Roe overturned. Before the 2022 Dobbs ruling, numerous law professors filed amicus briefs urging the Court to uphold Roe, and many legal scholars fiercely criticized the decision. PolitiFact rated the claim False. Trump also overstated that Roe's end left abortion 'where everybody wanted it from a legal standpoint' — polls show most Americans opposed its reversal.

lie: The Democrats are the radical ones on this position because they support abortion up to and even beyond the ninth month, the concept of having an abortion in the later months and even execution after birth. … The baby is born, the baby is executed after birth.
fallacy: Falsehood / Straw Man — No state allows killing a newborn. Infanticide is illegal in all 50 states, and 'execution after birth' is not a recognized position or practice. Late-term abortions occur only in rare, dire medical circumstances. PolitiFact rated the 'execution after birth' claim False, noting it fabricated a Democratic position that does not exist.

lie: I didn't know she was Black until a number of years ago, when she happened to turn Black, and now she wants to be known as Black. So, I don't know, is she Indian or is she Black?
fallacy: Falsehood / Misrepresentation — At the National Association of Black Journalists convention, Trump falsely suggested Kamala Harris only recently 'became' Black. Harris has always identified as both Black and Indian American; she attended a historically Black university and served in the Congressional Black Caucus. Her father is Jamaican, her mother Indian. PolitiFact, CNN, FactCheck.org and AP all debunked the claim.

lie: I had no inflation, virtually no inflation. They had the highest inflation perhaps in the history of our country. … We had the greatest economy in the history of our country.
fallacy: Falsehood / Exaggeration — Inflation was not zero under Trump (CPI rose 7.6% over his term, ~1.9% a year), and Biden-era inflation peaked at 9.1% in 2022 — far below the double-digit rates of the 1970s and early 1980s. GDP also grew faster under Clinton and Reagan; the economy shrank 2.2% in Trump's final year. Snopes and FactCheck rated the claims False.

lie: I'll get the war with Ukraine and Russia ended. If I'm president-elect, I'll get it done before even becoming president.
fallacy: Overreach / False Promise — Trump repeatedly (CNN counted dozens of times) promised to end the Russia-Ukraine war within 24 hours or before taking office. The war continued well past his January 2025 inauguration and first day in office. No mechanism was offered for delivering peace on that timeline, and his own officials later abandoned the 24-hour framing.

lie: And, above all, China is operating the Panama Canal.
fallacy: Falsehood / Misrepresentation — In his inaugural address, Trump claimed China operates the Panama Canal. Panama has owned and administered the canal since Dec. 31, 1999, via the autonomous Panama Canal Authority. Chinese influence is limited to a Hong Kong-based firm operating two ports at the canal's ends, while authority over the waterway remains with the Panamanian government.

lie: We will tariff and tax foreign countries to enrich our citizens.
fallacy: Falsehood / Misrepresentation — Trump's inaugural claim that tariffs fall on foreign countries is backwards. U.S. importers pay customs duties, and the cost is largely passed to American consumers as higher prices. Economists and the Tax Foundation found first-term tariffs were 'passed almost entirely through to US firms or final consumers,' making them a regressive tax on U.S. households.

lie: I changed the Obama policy, and we had a very good policy. … And then Biden came in and he changed it.
fallacy: Falsehood / False Cause — Hours after the deadly Washington air crash, Trump blamed FAA diversity hiring, claiming he ended an Obama policy that Biden 'reinstated.' Trump actually expanded disability hiring in 2019, and Biden did not reinstate the hiring assessment Trump ended in 2018. Investigators found no evidence DEI policies caused the crash, which remained under investigation.

lie: You should have never started it. … You could have made a deal.
fallacy: Falsehood / Historical Revisionism — Trump echoed Kremlin talking points claiming Ukraine started the war with Russia. Russia launched an unprovoked full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, after Ukraine voted overwhelmingly for Zelenskyy in 2019. PolitiFact rated the claim Pants on Fire, and Ukraine's leader accused Trump of 'living in a disinformation space.'

lie: [Zelenskyy is] A Dictator without Elections.
fallacy: Falsehood / Misrepresentation — Trump called Ukraine's president a 'dictator without elections.' Zelenskyy was democratically elected in 2019 with over 73% of the vote; elections were suspended solely because martial law — imposed after Russia's invasion — legally forbids them, as in many wartime democracies. A Georgetown professor compared his case to Britain postponing elections during WWII.
